name: Mission Santa Clara, first site: church and sacristy (palisade)
shape_note: First site (Thamien), Jan 1777 - Nov 1779, on the Guadalupe near its confluence with Mission Creek; position = SCU Neatline exhibit point (Spearman's location near the N end of San Jose airport; never confirmed by archaeology - Cartier 1980 found nothing). Flooded 23 Jan 1779 (water ~3 ft deep in the houses, Hall 1871); Murguia stayed on at the ruined site until the move of 11 Nov 1779. Church and sacristy 6 x 20 varas.

name: Mission Santa Clara, third (Murguia) church
shape_note: Third (Murguia) site, CA-SCl-30, under the realigned El Camino Real at the NE corner of SCU (Neatline point = the commemorative park at 500 El Camino Real). Cornerstone 19 Nov 1781, church dedicated 16 May 1784: 'the east-west oriented (9 by 41 varas) adobe church and sacristy, and the north-south west adobe wing of the quadrangle'; tule roofs in the 1780s, tejas and ladrillos during the 1790s (Skowronek & Wizorek 1997). Vancouver (Nov 1792): buildings on the San Francisco plan, an incomplete square, 'interior oblong square ... one hundred and seventy feet long, and one hundred broad', upper storeys used as granaries (Hall 1871 quoting Vancouver; Bancroft i.724). Church on the north side of the court, wing positions ESTIMATED from these descriptions (Caltrans 1988-89 excavations, Hylkema 1995, not seen). Damaged by the 1812 and 1818 earthquakes; as each building of the new quadrangle was finished its tiles were taken and the walls melted (stubs c.1880). Church 9 x 41 varas until it was lengthened in 1795; wall height ESTIMATED ('long and lofty', Vancouver).

name: Mission Santa Clara: new padres' house on higher ground (1791-97)

Position ESTIMATED west of the church.

name: Mission Santa Clara neophyte rancheria, adobe row 1 of 5 (1790s)
shape_note: Neophyte adobe row houses ('several continuous rows of homes built in 1792-1800 as dwellings for the Indian families', CHL 249 plaque; 'fourteen of these dwellings, thatched, were completed in 1793, nine more in 1794, and before 1798 nearly all the married neophytes were thus accommodated'; tile roofs by 1798 - Bancroft i.725 n.62). The City of Santa Clara describes five parallel rows west of the Murguia church; SCU excavations 2012-15 under the Dowd Art building and parking structure (Franklin St) found adobe house foundations, hearths and pits of ca.1780-1840s (Hylkema/Panich), and a cobble foundation in line with the Pena (Woman's Club) adobe (Skowronek & Wizorek 1997). Row layout ESTIMATED: rows parallel to the surviving adobe (bearing 66), ~25 m apart, ~6 m deep, units ~6 m wide. Rows 'gradually demolished and replaced with wood frame homes' after the Gold Rush; end years ESTIMATED.

name: Mission Santa Clara, fourth (temporary) church, later boys' dormitory and dance hall
shape_note: Adobe church hurriedly built east of the new construction site after the 1818 earthquake (1818-19 Informes: finished with ladrillos and tejas; Bancroft ii.377: 'a fine new church of adobes with tule roof' completed in 1817-18); the 1854 Black plat shows it 30 x 94 ft with a porch along the whole west wall. Church Dec 1819 - Aug 1825, then dormitory for neophyte boys, then (after 1836) home of Candelaria and her dance hall; bought by Santa Clara College 1860, demolished 1867. Rediscovered 1995 (cobble sacristy foundations 8 m apart; only photo early 1860s). Position = SCU Neatline point (St. Ignatius Gardens, across old Alviso St); long axis N-S on the campus grid (ESTIMATE). Height ESTIMATED from the gabled roofline in the photo.

name: Mission Santa Clara, 1822-25 quadrangle: east range (convento)
shape_note: 1822-25 quadrangle at 'Mission Heights' (today's SCU core). The church is the landmark model mission_santa_clara_1825; the 'Faculty Club' (Adobe Lodge, 1822) and an adobe wall SURVIVE and are today's buildings (known_building_dates_region.csv). The other adobe buildings 'were gradually demolished to make room for classrooms and dormitories'; a three-storey Jesuit faculty residence was built during the Civil War on top of an adobe wing (Skowronek & Wizorek 1997). Range positions ESTIMATED: a court between the church's SSE side and the Adobe Lodge (whose long axis runs 157 deg), LOW CONFIDENCE (1854 Black plat and Hendry & Bowman 1940 not seen). End = Civil-War-era faculty residence built over an adobe wing (ESTIMATE that it was this one).

shape_note: Built 1798, standing unchanged from at least 1818 until pulled down in 1850 (its adobes went into Hoppe's store at Market & Santa Clara). One storey, three rooms (court in the middle, alcalde east, jail west), gable ends facing east and west; on Market St at the corner of El Dorado St (now Post St) (Hall 1871). US flag raised over it by Fallon, July 1846. Size ESTIMATED from three rooms.

name: First St. Joseph's chapel (adobe, tule roof)
shape_note: Cornerstone 12 Jul 1803 (Viader; Estudillo as proxy sponsor); 'made of adobes, but covered with a tule roof'; walls cracked by the earthquake of late 1804; stood until 1835 (Hall 1871 pp.87-90; Bancroft ii.135). name: St. Joseph's church of 1835 (adobe)
shape_note: Built 1835 'on the very spot where the old one stood' under alcalde Antonio M. Pico with Antonio Sunol; encased in brick with two towers in 1858 (Hall 1871 p.122); damaged in the 1868 earthquake; the present cathedral replaced it 1876-77 (CHL 910). End = 1868 earthquake (ESTIMATE). Size ESTIMATED.

name: Luis Maria Peralta Adobe

Start = move of the pueblo (ESTIMATE). Prefer dating today's footprint.

name: Roberto-Sunol Adobe (Rancho de los Coches)

shape_note: Two-storey 40 x 60 ft adobe on the east side of Market Square (built 1849 by Sainsevain & Rochon as a hotel 'between the two adobe houses', Hall 1871; Assembly upstairs, Senate in the largest of four ground-floor rooms from 28 Dec 1849, Arbuckle 1985). name: Mission San Jose: first wooden church with grass roof

Langsdorff (May 1806): 'the buildings and grounds are already of very considerable extent ... most of their buildings are of brick [adobe]. The habitations of the Indians, las Rancherias, are not yet finished, so that at present they live chiefly in straw huts of a conical form' (Bancroft ii.139-140). Neophytes 286 (1800), 545 (1810), largest 1,886 (1831), 580 (1840); 1837 inventory: buildings incl. corrals $10,700, orchard and vineyard of 6,000 vines and ~600 fruit trees (Bancroft iii.725 n.). Enramada 10 Jun 1797; Amador's soldiers then cut timber and 'prepare[d] the necessary buildings'; 'a wooden structure with grass roof served as a church' until the adobe church of 1809 (Bancroft i.555-556). Position ESTIMATED behind the adobe church.

Number, size, position (west of today's Mission Blvd) and dates ESTIMATED by analogy with Mission Dolores (8 rows) - LOW CONFIDENCE. Rows decayed after secularization (1836-37) and the dispersal of the community in the 1840s.

name: Mission San Rafael: the 1818 adobe (chapel, padre's house, hospital rooms)
shape_note: Founded 14 Dec 1817 as an asistencia (hospital) of San Francisco at the place called Nanaguani; full mission 1822. 'In 1818 an adobe building 87 feet long, 42 feet wide, and 18 feet high had been erected; divided by partitions into chapel, padre's house, and all other apartments required, and furnished besides with a corridor of tules' (Bancroft ii.330); a church was added at one end the following year (secondary). Neophytes ~230 at founding, 590 (1820), 1,140 (1828), ~500 (1834), 195 at the mission (1839). Abandoned by 1844, used by Fremont 1846, a parish church built near the old chapel ruins in 1861, the remaining ruins removed 1870 ('most obliterated' mission). Placed at the 1949 replica chapel (landmark mission_san_rafael, 5th Ave & A St), which is said to stand on the hospital site; building arrangement ESTIMATED (HALS CA-87 not seen). Long axis along 5th Ave (ESTIMATE).

Three ranges around a ~25 m plaza, sizes and exact position ESTIMATED.

name: Sanchez Adobe (Rancho San Pedro)
shape_note: SURVIVES (CHL 391, 1000 Linda Mar Blvd, Pacifica; Overture/OSM footprint 23 x 9.7 m). Built 1842-46 by Francisco Sanchez, alcalde of San Francisco and grantee of Rancho San Pedro, probably with bricks of the old outstation; remodelled by Gen. Edward Kirkpatrick from 1871; county museum since 1947. Start = completion. Prefer dating today's footprint.

name: Pruristac, Aramai Ohlone village in San Pedro Valley
shape_note: Domed/conical tule-thatched family house on a bent-willow pole frame, about 3-5 m across (as in early_sf.csv; Milliken 2009 ch.3). Count is an ESTIMATE at ~6-8 people per house. Village of headman Yagueche (Mossues), visited by Portola's party 31 Oct 1769; the Aramai of Pruristac and Timigtac were no more than ~53 people and moved to Mission Dolores 1779-86 (Milliken 2009 App. B); a shell midden near the park ranger building marks it. Position ESTIMATED within the park.

name: Hospice / outpost of Mission Dolores at San Mateo
shape_note: Adobe hospice on El Camino Real on the north side of San Mateo Creek, 'built around 1800 by the Spanish Padres ... to break the journey from Santa Clara and serve the Indians of Mission Dolores' (CHL 393 marker at Baldwin/Baywood & El Camino Real); a grain station/granary there in the 1790s per other accounts; badly damaged by the 21 Oct 1868 earthquake and gone (USGS OFR 2008-1121). Size, orientation and exact point ESTIMATED.

name: Siplichiquin, Urebure Ohlone village at San Bruno
shape_note: Domed/conical tule-thatched family house on a bent-willow pole frame, about 3-5 m across (as in early_sf.csv; Milliken 2009 ch.3). Count is an ESTIMATE at ~6-8 people per house. 'born at San Bruno, the place called by the natives Siplichiquin'; a single bay-shore village group of ~40 people, absorbed into Mission Dolores by 1785; the Rivera-Palou party camped near it at the mouth of Colma Creek in Dec 1774 (Milliken 2009). Position ESTIMATED on the c.1800 bay edge near Colma/San Bruno creeks.

name: Ssalson Ohlone villages on lower San Mateo Creek (Uturbe, Altagmu)
shape_note: Domed/conical tule-thatched family house on a bent-willow pole frame, about 3-5 m across (as in early_sf.csv; Milliken 2009 ch.3). Count is an ESTIMATE at ~6-8 people per house. The Ssalsons (~210 people) lived in at least three villages 'along branches of the Arroyo of San Matheo' - Altagmu, Aleitac, Uturbe - and moved seasonally (Milliken 2009 App. B); Anza/Font passed a village on San Mateo Creek in Mar 1776. Most went to Mission Dolores 1780-93. Positions ESTIMATED along the creek.

name: Ssalson Ohlone village in the San Andreas Valley (Aleitac?)
shape_note: Domed/conical tule-thatched family house on a bent-willow pole frame, about 3-5 m across (as in early_sf.csv; Milliken 2009 ch.3). Count is an ESTIMATE at ~6-8 people per house. Palou (Nov 1774) found five 'large' villages in the San Andreas valley where Portola had seen none in 1769 (Milliken 2009 ch.3). Position ESTIMATED near the head of San Mateo Creek.

name: Lamchin Ohlone village on Laurel Creek (Belmont)
shape_note: Domed/conical tule-thatched family house on a bent-willow pole frame, about 3-5 m across (as in early_sf.csv; Milliken 2009 ch.3). Count is an ESTIMATE at ~6-8 people per house. Font's diary (Mar 1776): a Lamchin village on Laurel Creek in present Belmont whose people showed an arrow wound and warned of the Ssalsons (Milliken 2009). Lamchin ~240 people; most to Mission Dolores 1784-93. Position ESTIMATED on lower Laurel Creek.

name: Cachanigtac ('Las Pulgas'), Lamchin Ohlone village
shape_note: Domed/conical tule-thatched family house on a bent-willow pole frame, about 3-5 m across (as in early_sf.csv; Milliken 2009 ch.3). Count is an ESTIMATE at ~6-8 people per house. name: Ssiputca, Puichon Ohlone village on San Francisquito Creek
shape_note: Domed/conical tule-thatched family house on a bent-willow pole frame, about 3-5 m across (as in early_sf.csv; Milliken 2009 ch.3). Count is an ESTIMATE at ~6-8 people per house. The Puichon were the largest west-bay local tribe; their San Francisquito Creek village Ssiputca appears six times in the Mission Dolores registers, and Font (1776) reported a 'large' village of ~250 people on the creek (Milliken 2009). Position ESTIMATED on the creek near El Palo Alto; end ESTIMATED (baptisms 1781-1805).

name: Oljon Ohlone village at San Gregorio Creek
shape_note: Domed/conical tule-thatched family house on a bent-willow pole frame, about 3-5 m across (as in early_sf.csv; Milliken 2009 ch.3). Count is an ESTIMATE at ~6-8 people per house. Portola's party stayed two days with the Oljons at San Gregorio Creek (Oct 1769), who 'gave a festive welcome'; ~157 Oljons, most baptized 1786-93 (Milliken 2009). Position ESTIMATED on the lower creek.

name: Ohlone village at the mouth of Tunitas Creek

name: Ssatumnumo, Chiguan Ohlone village (Princeton)

name: Chagunte, Chiguan Ohlone village (Half Moon Bay)

'About a league hither' from Ssatumnumo, perhaps at present Half Moon Bay; Palou (Dec 1774) described a hamlet there built 'in the arroyo itself, on a thick wall that it forms like an island' (Milliken 2009). Position ESTIMATED on Pilarcitos Creek.

name: Mitenne, Quiroste Ohlone village at Whitehouse Creek (Ano Nuevo)
shape_note: Domed/conical tule-thatched family house on a bent-willow pole frame, about 3-5 m across (as in early_sf.csv; Milliken 2009 ch.3). Count is an ESTIMATE at ~6-8 people per house. Quiroste village of Mitenne near Point Ano Nuevo, visited by Portola 23 Oct 1769; 'large' (~200 people) at Whitehouse Creek per Crespi; Quirostes resisted under Charquin in the early 1790s and went mostly to Santa Clara (Milliken 2009). name: Charles Brown's sawmill on Alambique Creek (Woodside)

name: Peralta vaquero shelter (log and earth), Rancho San Antonio
shape_note: Rancho San Antonio, granted to Luis Maria Peralta 1820; his son Antonio's hacienda on Peralta Creek, today's Peralta Hacienda Historical Park (CHL 925, 2465 34th Ave). Peralta Hacienda chronology: c.1820 log-and-dirt vaquero shelter; 1821 first adobe 42 x 18 ft (survived 1856 and 1868, razed 1897); 1840 larger adobe 40 x 60 ft near it (destroyed Oct 1868); 1840 adobe wall 6-8 ft high enclosing ~2.5 acres with one-storey lean-to houses for visitors and laborers along its inside, ~27 by 1855; the 1868 earthquake 'destroyed the 1840 adobe and the adobe wall with its 22 lean-tos'. Positions inside the park ESTIMATED (the 1870 house stands near the adobes).

name: Vicente Peralta's adobe of 1847-48: side wings
shape_note: Vicente Peralta's Temescal home on Temescal Creek, at today's Vicente Way / 55th St & Telegraph (Oakland Wiki; marker 'Vicente Peralta's Chosen Place'). Peralta Hacienda chronology: 1836 first adobe 40 x 40 ft (Domingo lived there too), removed late 1880s; 1847-48 last adobe with three wings and a chapel serving all the Peraltas, burned 1866, removed in the 1880s. Layout ESTIMATED.

name: Domingo Peralta adobe on Codornices Creek (first Berkeley adobe)
shape_note: Domingo Peralta's 30 x 18 ft adobe on Codornices Creek (1841 or 1842), cracked in 1856 and razed after the 1868 earthquake (Peralta Hacienda chronology; Bowman 1951 via USGS OFR 2008-1121). Site = 'First Berkeley Adobe Site', 1304 Albina Ave (OHP BERD, point ESTIMATED on Albina Ave).

name: Ygnacio Peralta's first adobe (San Leandro)
shape_note: Ygnacio Peralta's first adobe, 42 x 18 ft, in the southern portion of Rancho San Antonio (1835), later given to his son Francisco (Peralta Hacienda chronology). Position near his later houses by San Leandro Creek ESTIMATED; end ESTIMATED.

name: Ygnacio Peralta's adobe facing San Leandro Creek
shape_note: Second adobe, 80 x 40 ft, facing San Leandro Creek, removed between 1874 and 1878 (Peralta Hacienda chronology); his 1860 brick house (CHL 285, 561 Lafayette Ave, Alta Mira Club) survives nearby. Position ESTIMATED.

name: Estudillo family home (Rancho San Leandro)
shape_note: Site of the last home, built about 1850, of Jose Joaquin Estudillo, grantee of Rancho San Leandro (1842), and Juana Martinez de Estudillo, whose family founded San Leandro (CHL 279, 550 W Estudillo Ave). Material, size and end ESTIMATED.

name: Guillermo Castro's adobe (Rancho San Lorenzo)
shape_note: Don Guillermo Castro's rancho adobe 'stood on the present site of City Hall' on Mission Blvd (marker; City of Hayward history); grant 1841/1843. End ESTIMATED (1868 Hayward earthquake; Castro had lost the rancho by the 1860s).

name: Guillermo Castro's corral (Hayward Heritage Plaza)
shape_note: 'Original site of corrals of Don Guillermo Castro' (marker); the city says the corral site is today's Heritage Plaza and Arboretum. Fence outline; size, position and end ESTIMATED.

name: Jose Maria Amador's first house at Alamilla Spring (Dublin)
shape_note: In 1826 Amador built his home at Alamilla Spring, on what became the NW corner of Dublin Blvd and San Ramon Rd (marker / City of Dublin); Rancho San Ramon granted 1834-35. Material, size and end ESTIMATED.

name: Jose Maria Amador's two-storey adobe (Rancho San Ramon)
shape_note: A two-storey adobe of Jose Maria Amador on the rancho, reportedly destroyed in the 1868 Hayward earthquake (Wikipedia 'Dougherty, California' / Rancho San Ramon). Start, size and position ESTIMATED (near his first house).

name: Francisco Solano Alviso Adobe ('El Alisal')
shape_note: SURVIVES (CHL 510, Alviso Adobe Community Park, 3459 Foothill Rd, Pleasanton). Built 1844-46 by Francisco Solano Alviso, 'the first adobe house to be built in the Pleasanton Valley', called El Alisal (the sycamores); Fremont's headquarters after the battle of Sunol Canyon (1846). Original footprint ESTIMATED (Overture footprint 27 x 15.7 m incl. later parts) - prefer dating today's footprint.

name: Francisco Maria Castro adobe (Rancho San Pablo)
shape_note: Don Francisco Castro (provisional grant of Rancho San Pablo 1823) built an adobe 'on the banks of Wildcat Creek at what is now the southwest corner of San Pablo Avenue and Church Lane'; 'erected before 1829' (Huntington Library photo record); deteriorating after his death (1831), so his sons built a new one for their mother (San Pablo Historical Society). Start, end and size ESTIMATED.

name: Alvarado Adobe (Gabriela Berryessa de Castro adobe), San Pablo
shape_note: Built 1842 by Jesus Maria Castro for his mother Gabriela Berryessa de Castro; from 1851 the home of Martina Castro and Gov. Juan Bautista Alvarado (CHL 512, NW corner San Pablo Ave & Church Ln). Demolished Aug 1954; the replica of 1978 (Alvarado Square civic center) is today's footprint (28.9 x 15.2 m) - do not use it before 1978. Original size ESTIMATED.

name: Victor Castro adobe (El Cerrito adobe), Rancho San Pablo
shape_note: Built 1839 by Victor Castro on the north bank of El Cerrito Creek at the edge of Rancho San Pablo; one-storey casa of 1839 with wings added in the 1840s (El Cerrito Historical Society); later a roadhouse/casino; destroyed by fire 20 Apr 1956; site = west parking lot of El Cerrito Plaza (CHL 356 plaque on the south side of the Plaza). Size ESTIMATED.

name: Joaquin Moraga Adobe (Rancho Laguna de los Palos Colorados)
shape_note: SURVIVES (CHL 509, 24 Adobe Ln, Orinda; private). Rancho granted 1835 to Joaquin Moraga and Juan Bernal; the adobe was completed in 1841. Footprint ESTIMATED (Overture footprint 25.6 x 20.8 m with later additions) - prefer dating today's footprint.

name: Don Salvio Pacheco Adobe (Rancho Monte del Diablo), Concord
shape_note: SURVIVES (CHL 515, 1870 Adobe St, Concord). Salvio Pacheco, grantee of Monte del Diablo (1834), completed 'this two-story adobe, the first building to be erected in this valley' on 24 Jun 1835 (CHL text; some histories date the present house later). Footprint ESTIMATED from Overture (29.1 x 15.3 m) - prefer dating today's footprint.

name: Don Fernando Pacheco Adobe, Concord
shape_note: SURVIVES as reconstructed in 1941 (CHL 455; Contra Costa Horsemen's Association, 3119 Grant St, 'one-quarter mile north' of the marker). Built 1843 by Fernando Pacheco. Which of the Overture footprints at the site is the adobe is UNCERTAIN; size ESTIMATED.

name: Vicente Martinez Adobe (Rancho El Pinole)
shape_note: SURVIVES (CHL 511; John Muir NHS, 4202 Alhambra Ave; Overture/OSM 'Martinez Adobe' 18 x 12.2 m, two storeys). Built 1849 by Vicente J. Martinez on Rancho El Pinole (granted to Ignacio Martinez 1836/1842); sold 1853 to Edward Franklin. Prefer dating today's footprint.

name: John Marsh's adobe (Rancho Los Meganos)
shape_note: Dr John Marsh bought Los Meganos in 1837-38 and lived in an adobe of four rooms plus an attic near Marsh Creek, 'not far from a large Miwok Indian village', until his Stone House was finished in 1856; the adobe site lies within Marsh Creek State Historic Park a short distance from the Stone House (John Marsh House Trust). Position, size and end ESTIMATED.

name: Bay Miwok village on Marsh Creek near Los Meganos
shape_note: Domed/conical tule-thatched family house on a bent-willow pole frame, about 3-5 m across (as in early_sf.csv; Milliken 2009 ch.3). Count is an ESTIMATE at ~6-8 people per house. 'A large Miwok Indian village' near Marsh's adobe (John Marsh House Trust); Marsh employed local Indian labour. Group affiliation (Julpun/Volvon) and position ESTIMATED; end ESTIMATED.

name: Large Huchiun-Aguasto village between Rodeo and Pinole creeks
shape_note: Domed/conical tule-thatched family house on a bent-willow pole frame, about 3-5 m across (as in early_sf.csv; Milliken 2009 ch.3). Count is an ESTIMATE at ~6-8 people per house. The largest Bay Area village reported by Spanish explorers (~400 people), in Huchiun or Huchiun-Aguasto territory 'in the area where the Rodeo and Pinole creeks' run, reported by Canizares (1775) and Anza (1776); Milliken suggests a seasonal gathering place (Milliken 2009 ch.3). Position ESTIMATED near lower Pinole Creek; end ESTIMATED (moves to the missions c.1794-1804).

name: First houses and stores of Martinez (laid out 1849)
shape_note: Town laid out in 1849 on Rancho El Pinole and named for Ygnacio Martinez; county seat 1850 (places.csv / Wikipedia 'Martinez'). The number and form of buildings by 1850 are ESTIMATED (procedural); positions random near the old town centre.

name: Elam Brown's house and barn at Acalanes (Lafayette)
shape_note: Elam Brown bought Rancho Acalanes and settled there in 1848 (places.csv; Wikipedia 'Lafayette, California'). Buildings, sizes, position and end ESTIMATED.

name: Camilo Ynitia Adobe (Olompali)
shape_note: CHL 210 'Oldest house north of San Francisco Bay': long said to be built 1776 by Camilo's father, but OHP research indicates a two-part construction beginning in 1834 by Camilo Ynitia, Coast Miwok headman of Olompali and the only Native American to hold a confirmed Mexican land grant (Rancho Olompali, 1843). Enclosed in the later Burdell house; burned 1976 and survives as a ruin in Olompali State Historic Park. Size ESTIMATED; end = 1976 fire.

name: Olompali, Coast Miwok village
shape_note: Coast Miwok kotcha: conical house of tule slabs or redwood bark over a pole frame, ~3-5 m across (Wikipedia 'Coast Miwok', after Barrett 1908 / Kelly). Count is an ESTIMATE. Olompali (Barrett's Olompolli, NW of Novato) dates to ~500 AD and was a main centre by ~1200, possibly the largest Miwok village in Marin; Camilo Ynitia's people stayed through the Mexican period (Olompali occupied by Camilo since 1834, Bancroft iii.719 n.); the rancho was sold in 1852. Position ESTIMATED within the park; end ESTIMATED.

name: John Reed's sawmill (Rancho Corte Madera del Presidio)
shape_note: First sawmill in Marin, built by John (Juan) Reed about 1833-36 on the creek at today's Old Mill Park, Mill Valley (CHL 207); the present mill structure is a later reconstruction. Size and end ESTIMATED.

name: John Reed's adobe (Mill Valley)
shape_note: Reed built a one-storey 18 x 30 ft adobe home near the present intersection of La Goma Ave and Locke Ln, Mill Valley (Mill Valley Historical Society interpretive plaque). Date approximate (grant 1834; Reed d.1843); end ESTIMATED.

name: William A. Richardson's house, Rancho Saucelito
shape_note: Richardson moved his family from Yerba Buena to Rancho Saucelito in June 1841; one account places his adobe at today's Pine & Bonita, another describes a two-room wooden house on Whaler's Cove (Sausalito Historical Society). Material, size and end UNCERTAIN.

name: Liwanelowa, Coast Miwok village at Sausalito
shape_note: Coast Miwok kotcha: conical house of tule slabs or redwood bark over a pole frame, ~3-5 m across (Wikipedia 'Coast Miwok', after Barrett 1908 / Kelly). Count is an ESTIMATE. Barrett's list: Liwanelowa at present-day Sausalito. Position ESTIMATED; end = founding of Mission San Rafael (ESTIMATE).

name: Echa-tamal, Coast Miwok village at Nicasio
shape_note: Coast Miwok kotcha: conical house of tule slabs or redwood bark over a pole frame, ~3-5 m across (Wikipedia 'Coast Miwok', after Barrett 1908 / Kelly). Count is an ESTIMATE. name: Olema-loke, Coast Miwok village at Olema
shape_note: Coast Miwok kotcha: conical house of tule slabs or redwood bark over a pole frame, ~3-5 m across (Wikipedia 'Coast Miwok', after Barrett 1908 / Kelly). Count is an ESTIMATE. Barrett's list: Olema-loke at present-day Olema. Position ESTIMATED.

name: Bauli-n, Coast Miwok village near Bolinas
shape_note: Coast Miwok kotcha: conical house of tule slabs or redwood bark over a pole frame, ~3-5 m across (Wikipedia 'Coast Miwok', after Barrett 1908 / Kelly). Count is an ESTIMATE. Barrett's list: Bauli-n near Bolinas (origin of 'Baulines'). Position ESTIMATED.

name: Chokeche, Coast Miwok village near Novato
shape_note: Coast Miwok kotcha: conical house of tule slabs or redwood bark over a pole frame, ~3-5 m across (Wikipedia 'Coast Miwok', after Barrett 1908 / Kelly). Count is an ESTIMATE. Barrett's list: Chokeche near Novato. Position ESTIMATED.

shape_note: Coast Miwok kotcha: conical house of tule slabs or redwood bark over a pole frame, ~3-5 m across (Wikipedia 'Coast Miwok', after Barrett 1908 / Kelly). Count is an ESTIMATE.
